A.explanation: 30 J is too large for the $250 \, \Omega$ resistor and 2.5 V ignores both the terminal p.d. of about 10 V and the internal loss.

B.explanation: 30 J is too large for the external resistor; 7.5 V would correspond to only $18 \, \text{J}$ total energy for the $2.4 \, \text{C}$ charge.

C.explanation: 24 J is correct for the external resistor, but 10.0 V is only the terminal p.d. $IR$ and omits the $6.0 \, \text{J}$ lost in the internal resistance.

D.explanation: $I^2Rt = 24 \, \text{J}$ externally, and total $30 \, \text{J}$ for $2.4 \, \text{C}$ gives e.m.f. $12.5 \, \text{V}$.

hints: Convert the $40 \, \text{mA}$ current to $0.040 \, \text{A}$ and use it with the $250 \, \Omega$ external resistor and $60 \, \text{s}$ time to find the external heating.
Remember total chemical energy equals external $24 \, \text{J}$ plus the $6.0 \, \text{J}$ dissipated in the internal resistance.
Find the charge $Q = It$ moved in $60 \, \text{s}$, then use e.m.f. $= $ total energy $/ Q$.
walkthrough: Note the series current $I = 40 \, \text{mA} = 0.040 \, \text{A}$, external $R = 250 \, \Omega$, time $t = 60 \, \text{s}$, and internal dissipated energy $6.0 \, \text{J}$.
Energy in the external resistor is Joule heating $W_R = I^2 R t = (0.040)^2 \times 250 \times 60$.
Total energy supplied by the battery is $W_{total} = 24 + 6.0 = 30 \, \text{J}$, and charge moved is $Q = It = 0.040 \times 60 = 2.4 \, \text{C}$.
E.m.f. is energy per unit charge: $E = W_{total}/Q = 30 / 2.4 = 12.5 \, \text{V}$.
So energy $24 \, \text{J}$ and e.m.f. $12.5 \, \text{V}$. This is option D.
